title: T/F/NI + Vocabulary: The Woman Who Would Not Wash Up (poziom wojewodzki)

tasks.instruction: Przeczytaj ponizszy tekst. Zdecyduj, ktore zdania (1.1.–1.5.) sa zgodne z trescia tekstu (T – True), ktore sa niezgodne (F – False), a ktore zawieraja informacje niepodane w tekscie (NI – No Information). Nastepnie znajdz w tekscie wyrazy lub wyrazenia, ktore odpowiadaja definicjom podanym w punktach 1.6.–1.10. Wymagana jest calkowita poprawnosc ortograficzna odpowiedzi.
tasks.text:
THE WOMAN WHO WOULD NOT WASH UP

The story Josephine Cochrane told about herself began with a dinner party and a broken plate. The Cochranes entertained often in Shelbyville, Illinois, and the china they used had been in the family since the seventeenth century; when a servant chipped a piece of it, she is supposed to have gone into the kitchen to do the washing herself, found the job intolerable, and announced that if nobody else was going to invent a machine to do it, she would. Whether the sequence was quite that neat is doubtful - it reaches us largely through interviews she gave decades afterwards - but the machine is real enough.

What she designed in 1886 was not the first attempt. Earlier dishwashers existed and did not work, chiefly because they scrubbed. Cochrane's insight was that the dishes should be held still and the water should move. She measured her plates, saucers and cups, made wire compartments to fit each shape, mounted them in a wheel inside a copper boiler and drove a pump that fired hot soapy water up at them. The principle has not changed since. Every dishwasher sold today is a refinement of that arrangement.

Circumstances turned the idea into a business. Her husband died the year before the patent, leaving debts, and a woman of her age and position who suddenly needed money had few respectable options. She built the first machines in a shed behind the house with a mechanic she hired, and she sold them herself, calling on hotel managers in Chicago - an activity she described as the hardest thing she had ever done, harder by some way than the engineering.

The patent granted in December 1886 describes the machine in the flat language such documents demand, and it repays reading. It specifies the wire racks by the crockery each is meant to hold, insists that the water be delivered under pressure rather than by agitation, and provides for a hand crank so that the thing could be worked where there was no power - a concession to the fact that hardly any kitchen of the period had any. Those who saw it running were struck less by the cleaning than by the speed. The machine got through in two minutes what a kitchen hand needed the best part of an hour to do, and it did so without breaking anything, which was the complaint she had started from.

The market she found was not the one she had expected. Hotels and restaurants bought the machine at once: they washed enormous quantities of crockery, they paid people to do it, and the arithmetic was obvious. Households did not. The machines were large and expensive, few homes had water hot enough, and - the objection she reported most often, with visible irritation - many women told her that washing up was the part of the housework they did not mind. It took until the 1950s, long after her death, for the domestic dishwasher to become an ordinary household object.

Cochrane exhibited at the World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago in 1893, where her machine won an award and was used in several of the restaurants on the site. Her company continued after she died in 1913 and was eventually absorbed into a larger manufacturer whose name is still on kitchen appliances today. She was admitted to the National Inventors Hall of Fame in 2006, which is either a fitting tribute or a very slow one, depending on how you feel about the ninety-three years in between.

items.statement: Cochrane's machine was the first device ever built for washing dishes.
items.explanation: FALSE - 'What she designed in 1886 was not the first attempt. Earlier dishwashers existed and did not work'.

items.statement: She found selling the machines harder than designing them.
items.explanation: TRUE - Calling on hotel managers was 'the hardest thing she had ever done, harder by some way than the engineering'.

items.statement: The mechanic who helped build the first machines later became her business partner.
items.explanation: NO INFORMATION - The text says only that she hired a mechanic to help build them in a shed.

items.statement: Her company was still owned by her family when it was taken over.
items.explanation: NO INFORMATION - The text records that the company continued after her death and was later absorbed, but not who owned it.

items.statement: Cochrane learned engineering from her father before she designed the machine.
items.explanation: NO INFORMATION - Her measurements and her design are described, but the text says nothing about how she was educated.
